stories.title: Jurors in Lindsay Clancy trial deadlocked but judge asks them to keep trying
stories.summary: Clancy, a resident of Massachusetts, is facing murder charges for killing her three children at their family home in 2023. Her lawyer does not dispute that the 36-year-old former nurse killed the children, but argues that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time and was unable to distinguish right from wrong. After discussing the case for several more hours on Tuesday, jurors were sent home for the day and asked to return on Wednesday. "I just want to thank you for all your hard work and commitment so far in this case," the judge told jurors before sending them home. The Massachusetts mother is charged with three counts of first-degree murder, as the prosecution argues she made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them. The jury, made up of nine women and three men, began deliberating last week after hearing weeks of testimony from dozens of witnesses. On Tuesday, audible gasps could be heard in the courtroom as Judge William Sullivan read out a note from the jury indicating that it was deadlocked. Clancy, who was left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window shortly after the killings, appeared stoic as she sat in a wheelchair beside her lawyer. It is not uncommon for jurors in high-profile trials to struggle to reach a decision, and judges have protocols for such situations. A deadlock among the jury such as this one happens in "complex and emotionally charged trials", Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law, told the BBC. "If the deadlock persists, the judge might issue an additional 'dynamite' instruction [known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge in Massachusetts] to encourage the group to consider alternative perspectives and strive for an agreement while upholding their genuine convictions," Cucolo said. But it is "typically a last-ditch effort" from a judge, she said.

stories.title: Bessent says Strait of Hormuz would be 'worthless piece of water' as oil pipelines bypass it
stories.summary: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz will be "like a worthless piece of water" in two years as oil will be shipped through land-based pipelines, bypassing the crucial waterway. Bessent made the remarks during a fireside chat with FOX Business Network host Larry Kudlow at the Group of 20 finance ministers' meetings in Asheville, North Carolina, as Washington and Tehran have exchanged strikes, heightening tensions in the strait. "We can see the Iranians are trying to use the Strait of Hormuz as a choke point. It's not a choke point for the U.S., but it is a choke point for many other countries," the secretary said. "That will be bypassed in two years. In two years, the Strait of Hormuz will be like a worthless piece of water. Oil will be going on pipelines across the land," he added. During the Middle East war, Iran has effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial shipping route for oil, natural gas, fertilizer and other commodities. Disruptions to shipping in the strait have kept energy prices high, piling pressure on Washington ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November. Gulf countries and those that rely on the strait for energy imports have sought to reduce their reliance on the waterway as Iran strives to assert control over the strait, a pivotal source of leverage in the monthslong war with the United States. Meanwhile, U.S. Central Command said that its forces struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran following recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against U.S. troops in the Middle East. In a social media post, Trump said that the strikes were "large and powerful" and in retaliation for Tehran's "failed" attempt at adding sea mines to the strait, which he claimed currently has no mines.
